title: Indian Island Site
summary: In 2005, storm erosion at Indian Island County Park exposed ancestral burial material and artifacts. Shinnecock and Unkechaug people worked with public officials around repatriation and protection. Precise exposure locations remain withheld to protect ancestral burials.
map_geometry_source: Broad public orientation point for Indian Island County Park from OSM/Nominatim and Directus text; not a burial exposure or vulnerable shoreline.
why_this_matters: When a 2005 storm eroded the beach at Indian Island and exposed ancestral burials, the Shinnecock and Unkechaug Nations worked alongside local officials to respectfully repatriate the remains. This cooperative effort highlights the vital, ongoing responsibility of contemporary Indigenous communities to actively protect and honor their ancestral resting places.
history_content:
In 2005, Heavy rains and high waves uncovered what might be an important early American Indian burial site at Indian Island County Park in Riverhead, N.Y. The site was discovered by a park supervisor after the Peconic River bank eroded in stormy conditions.
Archaeologists said they found bones from at least two people believed to be American Indians buried at the site during the Early Woodland period, from 800 B.C. to A.D. 800. They also said they found several artifacts, including a pipe and fragments of a bowl. The remains were being examined by a forensic anthropologist. "The bones were in small pieces," David Thompson, vice president of the Suffolk County Archaeological Association, told Newsday. "They were obviously burnt. There were charred pieces of skull and small pieces of a jawbone. The fact that they were cremated is a holdover from a culture that immediately preceded the Early Woodland, which was called the Transitional Culture. Officials said they were uncertain what will happen to the site. 1
preservation_content: Indian Island carries public-park history alongside sensitive ancestral burial context. Burial exposure areas, vulnerable shoreline locations, and places where ancestral remains were found are not identified.
